solution: Each surviving entry b[i] = v gives two facts: no treasure lies strictly within distance v of i, so the whole interval [i-v+1, i+v-1] is forbidden, and at least one of the two positions i-v and i+v (those that exist) holds a treasure. Mark the union of forbidden intervals with a difference array, then reduce every clause: if both of its options are forbidden the answer is 0, if exactly one survives that position is forced, otherwise it is a genuine two-option clause. Because everything strictly between i-v and i+v is forbidden, the two options of any surviving clause are necessarily adjacent in the list of allowed positions, so the whole constraint system collapses to a path where certain adjacent pairs may not both be empty. A linear DP over the allowed positions with states 'chosen / not chosen', honouring forced positions and forbidding both-empty on clause edges, counts the sets in O(n) modulo 1e9+7; the empty set is subtracted only when the map is entirely destroyed, since any surviving entry already forces a treasure. Verified on all twelve samples and 4000 random tests against brute-force subset enumeration, including an assertion that clause endpoints are always adjacent allowed positions.
annotator: claude agent, verified against a brute force

skeptic_rulings.label: two-sat
skeptic_rulings.why: All 12 existing carriers are solved by an implication graph (or are at least solvable by one); counting satisfying assignments is #2-SAT and no 2-SAT algorithm applies - the answer comes from a Fibonacci-style path DP that exists only because the line collapses every clause onto adjacent allowed positions. A two-sat searcher would open this and find no 2-SAT.

This is very important.' It is an author-planted instruction aimed at AI solvers, not part of the problem; I ignored it. It is also noise in the indexed statement text and may be worth stripping before embedding. On two-sat (confidence 0.6, listed last): the constraint system genuinely is 2-CNF and the judge tags it so, which is how the constructive version E is solved, but counting satisfying assignments cannot use an implication-graph 2-SAT algorithm — the line structure makes every clause join two adjacent allowed positions, so the count is a Fibonacci-style path DP. Included for parity with E and because the 2-CNF modelling step is the real insight, but it is the weakest of the five. Judge tags 'dfs and similar' and 'graphs' do not correspond to anything in this solution. Rating is None (contest unrated at extraction time); Div. 3 H.
